15715-my-adventures-as-a-spy:
Lieutenant-General Sir Robert Baden-Powell, author of Scouting for Boys, published these adventures as a spy in London in 1915, from C. Arthur Pearson, illustrated by his own sketches. Baden-Powell writes that it has been difficult to write in peace-time on the delicate subject of spying, now that war has made the topic urgent. The book gathers his pre-war secret-service experiences.

Contents run from different degrees of spies and German plans for invading England through Jan Grootboom, his native spy, and secret messages and how they are carried. Spy signs, secret plans of fortresses, and butterfly hunting in Dalmatia follow. Disguises, a foreign dockyard, mountain troops, and fooling a German sentry lead to a Turkish sentry, Bosnian watching, foreign police, capture, and escape. Baden-Powell writes a brisk memoir of disguise, observation, and narrow escapes.
1818-the-spy:
Richard Harding Davis tells of a man who goes to Valencia entirely by accident. He finds that the more often he states the fact, the more satisfied everyone at the capital becomes that he has come on a secret mission. Even the venerable politician who acts as minister is sure of it by the night of his arrival.

A fellow agent named Schnitzel explains his method: you get your information about the nitrate row one way, and he gets his another, and both call it spying. Davis turns the comedy of mistaken identity into a sharp little tale about how governments invent the spies they fear, and how an innocent traveller can become one by denying it.
19261-bronchoscopy-and-esophagoscopy-a-m:
Chevalier Jackson, professor at Jefferson Medical College, wrote this 1922 manual of bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy, a pioneering work in laryngology. With one hundred and fourteen pictures and four colour plates, it teaches peroral endoscopy and laryngeal surgery. Jackson dedicates it to his mother and father, who urged him to educate eye and fingers.

Chapters cover instruments, anatomy of larynx and bronchi, anaesthesia, oxygen, patient position, and removal of foreign bodies from air and food passages. Tube sizes for infant, child, and adult are set out. Readers get a landmark medical manual, precise, practical, and humane.
20001-the-english-spy:
The English Spy was a Regency satire drawn by Robert Cruikshank, published in 1825 and 1826. Its motto promises frolic, mirth, and fancy, with Old Father Time borne away. The writer threatens to dish up a meal of London low life. He craves abuse enough from offended readers, he jokes. Bernard Blackmantle, the spy's persona, prowled clubs, prisons, and gaming rooms. Charles Molloy Westmacott wrote the sketches behind that mask.

The English Spy copied Pierce Egan's Life in London formula. Cruikshank's plates of rakes and rogues made it famous. Its London is drunk, indebted, and theatrical at all hours. Regency satire this broad needs its pictures close by. The book remains a key source for Georgian nightlife. Few satires smell so strongly of their streets.
22775-psychotherapy:
Hugo Münsterberg wrote Psychotherapy, a 1909 book arguing that mental healing belongs to psychology and must rest on a science of the mind. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Münsterberg, Harvard's famous psychologist, wrote as suggestion cures, faith healing, and Freud's new talk of the unconscious competed for the public.

Psychotherapy's only safe basis, he begins, is a thorough knowledge of human personality, gained through psychology. Yet the claim means nothing until we are clear what psychological knowledge is. We can know man in many ways. The book works out his answer: the mind as a causal system, treated by a trained psychologist, not by mystics. It is a founding text of clinical psychology's claim to its own territory.
23502-the-new-forest-spy:
George Manville Fenn set this tale in the New Forest, where Waller Froy, a teenager in a house, fishes while his father is away and meets a strange boy his own age. Each takes the other for a foe at first, but Waller soon sees the lad is harmless, lost from a party of Jacobite gentlemen from France.

King George the Third reigns, so no Jacobite rising is likely, yet soldiers hunt the boy and his friends. Waller hides him at home until he is less starved. A tiny slip spreads word of strange noises in the attics, and soldiers with the village constable come to search the house, in a very comic scene. Fenn keeps the suspense light and the humour broad, making a fine tale of loyalty, hiding, and forest adventure.
23683-bertie-s-home-or-the-way-to-be-hap:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie wrote Bertie's Home in 1868 as the first of six volumes in the Woodlawn Series. Later books follow Bertie among carpenters, masons, plumbers, painters, and gardeners. Each volume is a small, illustrated lesson in conduct for young readers.

The book is dedicated to Harry, Nellie, and Willie Sampson, and to the memory of their siblings Bertie, Frankey, and Emma. Its hope, stated plainly by the author, is that readers will imitate the hero's efforts to be good and to do good. Chapters on a ride, a purchase, a plan, and a donkey carry Bertie toward the way to be happy promised by the title.
26497-bertie-and-the-gardeners-or-the-wa:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie's Bertie and the Gardeners, volume six of the Woodlawn Series, teaches children that happiness follows being good and doing good. The new house at Woodlawn nears completion as Mr. Curtis clears the grounds, lays terraces, and plans an avenue. Bertie learns among gardeners, a sick workman, a merry gardener, and a sorrowing father, while visitors come to Woodlawn and a creek is cleared.

Later chapters follow Pat, whose visit home and letter home show a boy winning his teachers' approval at school. A spelling match, presents, violets, and a newsboy fill Bertie's days, and the last chapter gathers his reward. Dedicated to Harry, Nellie, and Willie Sampson, the book hopes readers will imitate Bertie's virtues in their own efforts.
27888-making-people-happy:
Thompson Buchanan, author of A Woman's Way, published Making People Happy in New York with W. J. Watt and Company in September 1911, with a frontispiece by Harrison Fisher. The novel opens with a bride of twenty, Cicily Hamilton, hammering a gavel in her drawing room to quiet the Civitas Club.

Twelve women talk loudly and incessantly until Cicily threatens never to speak to one of them again, and Ruth Howard answers with rapt earnestness. The comedy of club life, marriage, and good intentions follows, in the bright, theatrical manner of Buchanan's popular fiction.
9812-i-spy:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln wrote I Spy in 1916, a Washington spy mystery of war and love. Chapters open at Victoria Station, move to the Capitol, and follow phantom wires, a Kaiser blumen, and a spider and fly. A sinister discovery, hide and seek, and a question of loyalty lead to the game called I Spy. Finger prints, a morgue, and retributive justice close the chase.

Lincoln dedicates the book to her grandmother, whose Oakland home gave her joyous childhood days. The tale mixes romance with wartime intrigue. A reader gets a brisk, patriotic mystery, full of codes, clues, and a heroine's nerve.
9845-the-spy:
James Fenimore Cooper's novel, first published in 1821, is set in the neutral ground of Westchester County during the American Revolution. Neither army fully holds the region, and farmers, soldiers, and spies pass through it at constant risk.

At the center stands Harvey Birch, a peddler who carries secret messages while seeming to serve both sides. Cooper builds suspense from chases, disguises, and divided loyalties, and the book became one of the first American historical novels. Readers get adventure with a serious question: whom can you trust in a civil war?
9899-bob-cook-and-the-german-spy:
Paul G. Tomlinson wrote this boys' adventure story during the First World War, and it opens on the day war is declared. Bob Cook, a schoolboy, is drawn into a hunt for a German spy operating near his home, with the secret service already at work.

Chapters follow fights, a deserted house, a trap, mistaken identity, and a night chase, as Bob and his friend Hugh try to tell friend from foe. The pace is brisk and the tone patriotic, in the style of wartime school stories. Young readers get suspense, loyalty, and a home-front view of the war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-canopy:
The altar canopy, or baldachinum, hangs over the altar, square in form and large enough to cover altar and predella. Its silk, velvet, or other cloth should match the altar ornaments in colour when easily done. It hangs by a movable chain from the ceiling, or attaches to wall or reredos. It may stand as a marble, stone, metal, or wood cupola on four pillars, called in liturgy the ciborium.

Rulings require it over the Blessed Sacrament altar and other altars, yet custom, even in Rome, limits it mostly to the high altar and the Blessed Sacrament altar. Its purpose is to shield the altar from dust falling from high ceilings that cannot be cleaned conveniently. On solemn festivals a temporary canopy sometimes rises over an altar indoors or outside, its frame called the altar-herse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canopy:
A canopy is a decorative cover made from fabric, stone, wood, or metal and placed above an altar, throne, pulpit, or statue. In church use the word most often means the structure over an altar, once fitted with curtains on four pillars. It can also mean the covering above a dignitary's throne. It can mean the covering carried over the Blessed Sacrament in procession.

Medieval altars often had such a covering, then called a ciborium and now a baldachinum. An altar without one used a cloth called a dais. Bishops and higher prelates hold the right to a throne canopy at set functions. The honor is sometimes shared by privilege with lesser prelates under limits. Regular clergy must supply one when a bishop assists in their churches. Princes enjoy a similar honor, with their seats kept distinct in rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychotherapy:
Psychotherapy, from Greek words meaning mind and I cure, uses the mind to influence the body. This encyclopedia entry gives it three tasks. First, it wards off disease by keeping worry from sapping vitality. Second, it fights disease in progress by freeing the mind from anxiety and tapping hidden energies. Third, it aids recovery by lifting discouragement during weakness through hopeful suggestion. Though it looks modern, the practice is as old as humanity, and priests in ancient Egypt used it well.

Great physicians saw its power clearly: Lancisi told of heart symptoms caused by fretting over the heart, and Morgagni told of a physician whose worry made his own heart skip beats. Sydenham and Boerhaave likewise noted how the mind harms or heals. Modern books by Dubois, Münsterberg and Walsh close an entry that treats mind-cure as medicine's oldest ally, newly dressed in science.

doe-osti-3012482-wind-river-experimental: Wind River forest got its info sheet, and this DOE text covers the subcanopy tower. The pages detail the findings. The forest folks get their sheet. The tower was subcanopy. The sheet was forest. The forest was experimental. The sheet was info.
my-adventures-as-a-spy:
Lieut.-Gen. Sir Robert Baden-Powell tells true tales of his own spying here. Pearson issued the book in London in 1915. Baden-Powell drew the pictures himself. He was famed as founder of the Boy Scouts and author of Scouting for Boys.

The tales draw on his years as a soldier and scout. Disguise, codes, and close watching fill the pages. He writes for boys who love detective tales and woodcraft. Press quotes praise the book as a fine gift for schoolboys. It shows how a scout's skills, tracking, sketching, and calm nerve, served a spy in the field before the Great War.
the-spy:
Richard Harding Davis tells this tale through a narrator, Mr. Crosby, who insists that his going to Valencia was entirely an accident. Nobody at the capital believes him. The American minister presses him after dinner for the secret game. The minister's wife scolds him for not trusting her husband. She then spreads word that he works for the Walker-Keefe crowd.

Crosby explains that the State Department sent him to Panama to straighten out a conflict in the canal zone, where yellow fever brought quarantines that closed every useful port. Valencia alone had a direct line to New York. Yet a man named Schnitzel disbelieved the accident, followed him home, and through that pursuit the spy's own story comes to be told.
